pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5–Y6 'solve problems involving … scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): connects to 4.OA.2 (multiplicative comparison) and 6.RP.1–3 (ratios and unit rates) — this topic is the bridge from whole-number scaling to proportional reasoning.
• Operational details — two related structures: SCALING by a fraction (multiply a quantity by a fraction >1 or <1: enlarge/reduce; e.g. ×6/4 for the recipe, ×1/2 for the shape) and RATES (a per-unit relationship: £12 per 3 kg → £4 per kg → ×5). The powerful general strategy is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by the double number line and ratio table. Children must see scaling as multiplicative (a fraction/rate multiplier), not additive. This is the conceptual launchpad for ratio and proportion (a separate domain) and must stay grounded in known multiplicative-comparison ideas.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): scale a quantity by a simple whole factor and by 1/2 with a double number line. Tier B (age 9–10): solve a rate problem via the unitary method (3 kg=£12 → 1 kg=£4 → 5 kg=£20) and a fraction-scaling recipe problem. Tier C (age 10): choose unitary vs scale-factor efficiently and justify with a ratio table / double number line.
bestPractices: Teach the unitary method — find one unit then scale — as the reliable general strategy, supported by a double number line and ratio table.
Represent rates on a double number line (kg vs £) so the proportional (multiplicative) relationship is visible and both quantities scale together.
Treat scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction/rate), explicitly contrasting with additive change, to prevent the classic 'add the difference' error.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two quantities scaling together) — core rate/scaling tool
Ratio table — unit value and scaled values
Bar model — fraction scaling of a quantity
Scale-factor arrow (×6/4, ×1/2) linking original to scaled
commonMisconceptions: Scaling additively — adding the difference in people/kg instead of multiplying by the ratio (recipe for 6 = recipe for 4 + 2 portions of everything, done wrongly).
Not finding the unit value, so unable to scale to a new amount.
Inverting the rate (£12 per 3 kg treated as £3 per kg).
Confusing scaling up with down, or mis-applying ×1/2.
Treating rate problems as unrelated to multiplicative comparison / fractions.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds: solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (e.g. a recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → cost of 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2). The through-line is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by a double number line, ratio table and bar model. Learners should experience scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with the common additive 'add the difference' error, across authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes). Activities range from a manipulable double-number-line scaler that builds the proportional feel, through a Socratic unit-rate dialogue, a worked annotated exemplar, to checkable practice with targeted distractors.

activities.title: Double-number-line scaler: find one unit, then scale
feedback: When the child finds 1 kg = £4 and reaches £20 for 5 kg, affirm the unitary route: 'you found the cost of one, then multiplied by five'.

If the additive-trap attempt is tried, point out that adding the same number to both quantities (£12 + 2 = £14 for 5 kg) knocks the two lines out of alignment and gives a wrong amount. The rate holds only when each quantity changes by matching amounts (2 kg with £8), which is the same as scaling by the unit rate.
In recipe mode, if a learner adds 200 g for the '2 extra people', show that per-person is 50 g, so 6 people need 300 g, not 400 g.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation of two locked quantities makes the multiplicative nature of scaling tangible and exposes the unitary method; sliding one quantity and watching the other move proportionally helps learners feel why adding the same amount to both quantities breaks the relationship. The additive-trap comparison is one optional device for making the contrast visible, not a claim that only manipulation can teach this.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: On two parallel lines locked by a rate (e.g. kilograms against cost in pounds, £), slide to mark 3 kg opposite £12.
Use a 'find 1 unit' action to collapse the lines to 1 kg = £4, then slide on to 5 kg and read off £20.
Switch to a recipe mode: scale ingredients by ×6/4 (e.g. 200 g flour for 4 people → how much for 6?) shown on a bar model.
Switch to a shape mode: halve every dimension (×1/2) and read the new measurements.

Try the 'additive trap' toggle: add the same number to both lines (3 kg + 2 = 5 kg, so £12 + 2 = £14), then compare with the locked-rate result of £20. Notice that adding matching amounts instead (2 kg and its value, £8) keeps the lines aligned and gives £20.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling and rates are proportional, multiplicative relationships: finding the value of one unit unlocks any target amount, and adding the same difference to both quantities does not preserve the relationship.

activities.title: Unit-rate dialogue: 'what does one cost?'
feedback: If the learner gives the unit value and scales correctly, name the strategy: 'you used the unitary method'.
If the learner answers the additive-objection probe by defending adding 200 g, redirect to per-person value (50 g) and ask them to total for 6.
For the 4→10 stretch, confirm that per-person value scales to any target, unlike hunting for a whole-number factor.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue builds the unitary habit and can pose rich, varied contexts and challenge the additive misconception verbally. It cannot render a manipulable double number line, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive scaler.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: Respond to a market-trader or chef character posing rate and recipe problems: 'If 3 kg costs £12, what does ONE kilogram cost? So what about five?'
State the unit value aloud or in writing, then state how you scale it to the target amount.
Answer the probe 'Someone said 6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more — what's wrong with that?' and explain the flaw.
Tackle a stretch case ('a recipe for 4, but you need it for 10') and say whether the unit-value method still works.
activities.intendedInsight: Routing every proportional problem through 'the value of one, then times the target' is a reliable general habit that works even when the scale factor is not a whole number.

activities.title: Worked exemplar: annotated double number line and ratio table
feedback: After revealing each step, restate the move: 'divide by 3 to get one, then multiply by 5'.
Prompt the learner to apply the same two-step reveal to their own new problem rather than only reading the exemplar.
activities.rationale: A worked, tap-to-reveal exemplar is a useful reference for the structure of the method, but a fixed image cannot provide new problems to solve, so it should be paired with independent problem-solving.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: Study an annotated double number line (kg vs £) and a ratio table with a unit-value column.
Reveal the unitary steps one at a time: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = £4 → 5 kg = £20.
Read the ratio table to see the unit column (1 person = 50 g) and how scaled values follow from it.
Use the exemplar as a reference, then solve a new, different rate/scaling problem yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit value is the key column of a ratio table / anchor point of a double number line; scaled values are multiples of it.

activities.title: Checkable practice with additive-error distractors
feedback: For a chosen additive distractor, explain that it adds an amount that does not match the change (e.g. adding 200 g, the amount for 4 people, for only 2 extra people, or adding 2 to the quantity) rather than scaling; show the per-unit route: 50 g per person, so 2 more people need 100 g, giving 300 g.

If division is inverted (e.g. 4 ÷ 200 or 3 kg treated as £3 per kg), prompt labelling units (g per person, £ per kg) to orient the division and check the unit value is reasonable (50 g per person, not 0.02).
activities.rationale: Rate and scaling answers are checkable, so targeted distractors can verify the method and surface the additive and inversion misconceptions. This format is better suited to checking and diagnosing than to first building the proportional feel, so it works best after the interactive and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Fill in the unitary steps: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = □ → 5 kg = □.
Choose the correct recipe-for-6 amount from options that include an additive distractor (e.g. 400 g from 'add 200 g for 2 more people' vs the correct 300 g).
Select the correct multiplier for a scaling problem (e.g. ×6/4 = ×1.5, ×1/2).
Use a slider to set the scaled quantity and check it against the unit value.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct proportional answers come from multiplying the unit value or applying the right fractional multiplier; additive answers are identifiable errors.

constraints: Scaling must be taught as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with additive 'add the difference' change.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Include at least one non-integer scale factor (e.g. 4→6, factor 6/4) so learners cannot rely on whole-number multiples; the unit-value route always works.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness of the unit value (e.g. 50 g per person, not 0.02).
This topic is the launchpad for formal ratio and proportion (a separate domain); keep it grounded in known multiplicative-comparison and fraction ideas rather than introducing formal ratio notation.

The worked exemplar and quiz are scaffolds/checks: a fixed image and recognition items cannot by themselves elicit independent solving of new problems, so pair them with activities where the learner constructs the solution.

The 'additive trap' toggle and live sliders are optional devices for making the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and manipulation is not asserted to be the only way to learn this.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 200÷4 = 50 g per person, ×6 = 300 g (scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200×1.5 = 300) — correct; £12÷3 = £4 per kg, ×5 = £20 — correct. These match the source's correctAnswer.

The source lists an error pattern '200÷4 = 40' as an example of a performance slip; the correct value is 50. It is presented in the source as a learner error, not as a taught fact, so it is not reproduced as correct in any activity.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (CCSS bridge claim and NCETM guidance); the DfE claim is verified:true. No new verification is asserted here. The CCSS bridging claim was not used as a sourceClaim since no activity's rationale depends on it directly.

The DfE curriculum claim is a topic-level claim and was not attached to activities whose rationales turn on the multiplicative/unitary principle (activity 1) or answer-checkability (activity 4); the NCETM claim, which states the teaching principle, is used instead.
The source's artefact-fit note that '3D adds no proportional insight' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been omitted rather than asserted as universal.

Activity 4's rationale was softened from a categorical 'verifies rather than builds' to a relative affordance (better suited to checking than to first building the feel) to avoid an unsupported 'quiz only assesses' claim.

probeDeeper: How much flour would ONE person need? How did that help you get to 6?
Someone said '6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more'. What's wrong with that?
If 3 kg costs £12, what does 1 kg cost — and how do you know?
What if the recipe were for 4 people and you needed it for 10 — would your method still work?
assess.correctAnswer: Flour: 300 g (200 ÷ 4 = 50 g per person, × 6 = 300; or scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200 × 1.5). Cost: £20 (£12 ÷ 3 = £4 per kg, × 5 = £20). The teacher watches for a multiplicative route — unit rate or scale factor — not additive 'add 2 more people so add 200 g'.

errorPatterns.pattern: uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative — '6 is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g' giving 400 g, or 'add £12 again'
errorPatterns.nextMove: set up a ratio table (people | flour) and fill the unit column (1 person = 50 g) so scaling becomes 'per one, then times'; contrast with the wrong additive jump side by side.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child changes the quantity by the DIFFERENCE between the two situations rather than by a ratio

errorPatterns.pattern: finds the unit rate but then multiplies by the wrong quantity, or inverts the division (4 ÷ 200)
errorPatterns.nextMove: label units on every number (g per person) so the division is oriented correctly; check the unit rate is 'reasonable' (50 g per person, not 0.02).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides the wrong way (people by grams) or scales by the original count not the target

errorPatterns.pattern: can only scale by whole-number factors — stalls when 6/4 is not a whole multiple of 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: route through the unit value (per one person) which always works, rather than hunting for a whole-number scale factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child solves 3→6 (×2) confidently but freezes on 4→6

errorPatterns.pattern: sets up the proportion correctly but slips in the arithmetic (200÷4 = 40)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach proportion; have the child check the unit rate against the original (50 × 4 = 200?).

responseLevels.gap: scales additively (adds the difference) or inverts the rate; answer bears no multiplicative relationship to the given values.
responseLevels.full: routes reliably through unit rate or scale factor for both integer and non-integer cases, orients the division by units, and rejects additive scaling with a reason.
responseLevels.partial: solves whole-number-multiple cases (3→6) by scaling but stalls on non-integer factors (4→6), or finds a unit rate inconsistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child rate/scaling problems to solve, watching their method: 'A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?' and 'If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?' Watch whether they find a unit value or a scale factor, or whether they just add on a difference.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error in proportional reasoning is additive: '4→6 people is +2, so +2 of something'. Watching the method (unit rate vs adding a constant) reveals whether the child reasons multiplicatively. The non-integer scale factor (6/4) also catches children who can only scale by whole numbers.
